I was driving yesterday afternoon in a hansom cab down one of the sloping streets into the Strand, reading one of my own admirable articles with continual pleasure, and still more continual surprise, when the horse fell forward, scrambled a moment on the scraping stones, staggered to his feet again, and went forward. The horses in my cabs often do this, and I have learnt to enjoy my own articles at any angle of the vehicle. So I did not see anything at all odd about the way the horse went on again. But I saw it suddenly in the faces of all the people on the pavement. They were all turned towards me, and they were all struck with fear suddenly, as with a white flame out of the sky. And one man half ran out into the road with a movement of the elbow as if warding off a blow, and tried to stop the horse. Then I knew that the reins were lost, and the next moment the horse was like a living thunder-bolt. I try to describe things exactly as they seemed to me; many details I may have missed or mis-stated; many details may have, so to speak, gone mad in the race down the road. I remember that I once called one of my experiences narrated in this paper “A Fragment of Fact.” This is, at any rate, a fragment of fact. No fact could possibly be more fragmentary than the sort of fact that I expected to be at the bottom of that street.

.....

I believe in preaching to the converted; for I have generally found that the converted do not understand their own religion. Thus I have always urged in this paper that democracy has a deeper meaning than democrats understand; that is, that common and popular things, proverbs, and ordinary sayings always have something in them unrealised by most who repeat them. Here is one. We have all heard about the man who is in momentary danger, and who sees the whole of his life pass before him in a moment. In the cold, literal, and common sense of words, this is obviously a thundering lie. Nobody can pretend that in an accident or a mortal crisis he elaborately remembered all the tickets he had ever taken to Wimbledon, or all the times that he had ever passed the brown bread and butter.

But in those few moments, while my cab was tearing towards the traffic of the Strand, I discovered that there is a truth behind this phrase, as there is behind all popular phrases. I did really have, in that short and shrieking period, a rapid succession of a number of fundamental points of view. I had, so to speak, about five religions in almost as many seconds. My first religion was pure Paganism, which among sincere men is more shortly described as extreme fear. Then there succeeded a state of mind which is quite real, but for which no proper name has ever been found. The ancients called it Stoicism, and I think it must be what some German lunatics mean (if they mean anything) when they talk about Pessimism. It was an empty and open acceptance of the thing that happens—as if one had got beyond the value of it. And then, curiously enough, came a very strong contrary feeling—that things mattered very much indeed, and yet that they were something more than tragic. It was a feeling, not that life was unimportant, but that life was much too important ever to be anything but life. I hope that this was Christianity. At any rate, it occurred at the moment when we went crash into the omnibus.

message.content:
"Yesterday afternoon, I found myself riding in a hansom cab, gliding down one of the inclined streets leading to the Strand. I was engrossed in one of my own exceptional articles, experiencing both enjoyment and surprise, when suddenly the horse stumbled. It fell forward, scrambled momentarily on the rough stones, regained its footing, and continued on. This was not an unusual occurrence for the horses in my cabs, and I had grown accustomed to appreciating my articles from any angle of the vehicle. Thus, I did not initially perceive anything peculiar about the horse’s recovery. However, the expressions of the pedestrians on the sidewalk caught my attention. They were all gazing at me, their faces marked by an abrupt fear, as if struck by a flash of lightning. One man even stepped into the street, his elbow raised as if to deflect an impending blow, attempting to halt the horse. In that instant, I realized the reins had slipped away, and the next moment, the horse transformed into a force of nature, akin to a living thunderbolt. I strive to convey my experiences with precision, though I may have overlooked or misrepresented some details, as they may have become distorted in the chaos of the moment. I once referred to an experience in this paper as “A Fragment of Fact.” This moment, at least, qualifies as a fragment of fact, and no fact could be more fragmented than what I anticipated at the end of that street.

I firmly believe in addressing those already aligned with my views; I have often found that these individuals do not fully grasp their own beliefs. Consequently, I have consistently advocated in this paper that democracy encompasses a more profound significance than what its proponents recognize. Common and popular expressions, proverbs, and everyday sayings often contain deeper meanings that escape the understanding of many who utter them. One such notion is the idea of a person facing imminent peril who perceives the entirety of their life flashing before them in an instant. In the stark, literal sense, this assertion is undeniably a grand falsehood. No one can claim to remember every ticket purchased for a trip to Wimbledon or every instance of passing around brown bread and butter during a moment of crisis.

Yet, during those fleeting moments while my cab hurtled toward the bustling traffic of the Strand, I uncovered a deeper truth behind this notion, as there is often a kernel of truth within popular sayings. In that brief, tumultuous span, I experienced a rapid succession of several core perspectives. In what felt like mere seconds, I transitioned through what could be described as five distinct religions. My initial perspective was one of sheer Paganism, which among earnest individuals is more succinctly defined as profound fear. This was soon followed by a mental state that is undeniably real, yet lacks a proper designation. The ancients referred to it as Stoicism, and it resembles what some German thinkers might mean (if they have any meaning at all) when discussing Pessimism. It represented an empty and open acceptance of events as they unfold, as if one had transcended their intrinsic value. Curiously, I then experienced a strong counter-emotion—that things held significant importance, yet were also something beyond mere tragedy. It was not that life was trivial; rather, it felt overwhelmingly significant, too vital to ever be reduced to anything less than life itself. I hope this sentiment reflected what one might call Christianity. At any rate, it surfaced just as we collided with the omnibus."
